title: Proof pages for a community sports club
metaTitle: Proof pages that help a member join
excerpt: A club proof page should show a constraint, the decision, and people playing, then how a similar member sees membership or the schedule. Medals alone are decoration.
primaryKeyword: community sports club case study page
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. A decision being made in the open, which is what a proof page should show.
caption: A person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs at the start of a club proof page?
faqs.answer: Start with the constraint. Say who was stuck, what was scarce, and what the club refused to keep doing. A reader who recognizes that stuck-ness will stay. A trophy in the first sentence tells them the page is for insiders.

faqs.question: Are screenshots evidence?
faqs.answer: A screenshot is evidence only when the timetable, or some other visible rule, is the decision. Crop to the part that changed. A full-window capture of a homepage proves that a website exists, which the reader already knows.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: End on the next member. Name the session to attend first, what to bring, and the link to membership or the schedule, in the same words as the rest of the site. A closing line about the journey continuing drops them back into fog.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A community sports club case study page should show a constraint, the decision the club made, and people playing, including how a new person starts. Screenshots of a website, or a gallery of medals, are decoration until a decision is visible. Close the page by showing how a similar member can see membership or the schedule.

One season, told plainly, is more useful than a decade summarized as excellence. The reader is deciding whether to join. They are borrowing your last hard choice as evidence that the club is run on purpose.

## Start from the constraint

Name the limit before you name the pride. The hall was only free after 8 p.m. The junior list had outgrown one coach. Beginners were arriving and leaving because the social session assumed everyone knew the rules. The women's side had interest and no separate hour. A constraint is a fact that made the old setup fail someone.

Write it in the first screen, in two or three sentences. Who was stuck. What was scarce. What would have happened if the club had done nothing. A reader who recognizes their own stuck-ness will stay. A reader who meets a trophy in sentence one will assume the page is for insiders.

Google's notes on [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) ask whether you can show how something was produced, the way a good review shows what was tested and what the evidence was. A club proof page has a "how" as well. How you noticed the problem. How you chose. What you refused to pretend. Process is allowed to be ordinary. Ordinary process is credible.

Avoid a fake crisis. If the constraint was mild, say so. "We had a free court and a list of beginners, and no format that fit both" is a real problem. Inflating it into a rescue story makes the rest of the page harder to trust.

## The decision, in the club's actual options

Show the choice. You could have told beginners to watch for a month. You opened a four-week course instead, on the same night, with a named coach, and a rule that the course feeds the social session. You could have stretched one junior coach across forty children. You capped the group and opened a second hour. The decision includes what you declined.

A decision has a cost. The second hour costs hall hire. The course costs a coach who is no longer playing that night. The cap disappoints someone on the waiting list. Mention the cost in a sentence. Clubs that only publish the happy outcome sound like advertisements. Clubs that mention the tradeoff sound like they are in charge of their week.

Keep the decision specific enough that another club could learn from it, and specific enough that a potential member can see the result in the current offer. "We redesigned our pathway" is not a decision. "Beginners spend four Tuesdays with Coach Ahmed, then join the 8 p.m. social" is a decision. It also tells the reader how to start.

If the decision is still in force, link to the live version. The course dates. The junior cap. The fees for that offer. A proof page that describes a program you no longer run is a history essay. Mark it as history, or update it. People will try to join the thing you described.

## People playing, and the first session

The evidence a member needs is people in the activity that resulted from the decision. Photograph the course, the second junior hour, the new social format. Show bodies doing the sport, at a distance where the format is legible. A circle of beginners listening. A game underway with mixed ability and an obvious host. A junior group small enough to match the cap you claim.

Pair the picture with a caption that states the fact. "Week two of the beginner course, same coach as week one." The caption is part of the proof. A poetic caption throws away the fact you took the picture to show.

Then write how a similar person starts, in the present tense. Email is the wrong default if the real door is the schedule. Say which session to attend first, what to bring, and what the first half hour will feel like. If the proof is about juniors, say what the parent does at drop-off. The reader should be able to imagine Tuesday, not just admire last Tuesday.

Ballarat Box Sports is a public example of a community sports brand site from Hanabi. Use that kind of reference as a reminder that a sports club can present itself as a brand with a point of view. A proof page is still about the club's decision, and it is about the people who play. It is a story of a choice. It is a door into the current week.

## Screenshots and medals are supporting cast

A screenshot of a timetable can support the story if the timetable is the decision. Show the before and after only if both are true and readable. Crop to the part that changed. A full-window capture of a website, with browser chrome and a heroic banner, proves that a website exists. The reader already knows that. They are on it.

Medals can appear once, late, if the decision was about a competitive side and the result included a competition. One image, with the year and the squad named. A gallery of cups without the constraint that preceded them is the trophy case again, moved to a URL that sounds like a case study. The person deciding whether to join still needs the door, the people, and the rule.

Quotes, if you use them, should come from a named member who agreed, and they should describe the decision. "I had not played since school, and the four-week course was the reason I stayed." That sentence is evidence. "Best club in the city" is a poster. Skip the poster. Do not write a quote the member did not say.

Numbers belong only when the club will stand by them. A waiting list of twelve. A course that ran three times last season. Leave out attendance figures you rounded for drama. An honest small number is stronger than a theatrical one, and this article will not invent one for you.

## End on the next member

The last section is practical. If you are new, start here. If you are a parent, start here. See membership or the schedule. Repeat the path in the same words as the homepage and the fees page, so the proof page feels like part of the same club.

Offer the closest live fact. The next course date. The night the social session runs. The age band for the junior hour you just described. A proof page that ends on "the journey continues" drops the reader back into fog at the moment they were ready.

Invite a question only for the case the page cannot cover. A player returning from injury. A parent of a child younger than the published age. Give one contact, and say who reads it. The primary action remains the schedule or the membership page. A form with ten fields is a poor ending to a story about making the club easier to enter.

If you have several proof pages, give each a distinct constraint. Beginners. Juniors. The competitive side. Three pages that all say "we are a family" will be skimmed as one page. Nielsen Norman Group's account of [time on page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a reminder that the first 10 seconds decide whether anyone reads the decision at all. Put the constraint in the title and in the first lines. "How we opened a beginner course on Tuesdays" is a title a person can use. "Our story of growth" is a title they can skip.

## Keep a proof page maintainable

Write it so a volunteer can update the date and the coach's name without breaking the layout. One column of prose, a few real photographs, a clear link. Avoid a design that only works if every season produces a professional photoshoot. Phone pictures from the session, taken with permission and in focus, are better evidence than a polished image of an empty hall.

Store the page where the club can find it later. Link it from the relevant offer on the services menu, not only from a hidden "news" item. A proof that nobody can reach from the beginner block is a diary entry.

Hanabi's studio practice on proof is the same shape: constraint, decision, and the work that resulted, told so a similar buyer can see themselves. For a club, the buyer is a member. The result they need to see is people playing, and a way to start this month.

## After the story, the map

A reader who believes the story will try to move around the site. The labels they meet should match the words they just learned: beginner course, social, juniors, fees, schedule. Navigation is that map, and it is the subject of [navigation for a community sports club](/blog/navigation-for-a-community-sports-club).

If you are planning a small set of pages and want to talk through the order, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one real constraint from last season, not a slogan.
